name: Science, STEM, and Computer Science
blurb: Before they had any lessons on the subject, 195 fifth and sixth graders in Finland were asked what artificial intelligence is. Their answers were varied and often confused.
title: Science, STEM, and Computer Science
answer: Before they had any lessons on the subject, 195 fifth and sixth graders in Finland were asked what artificial intelligence is. Their answers were varied and often confused.

papers.why: Shows K-12 AI curricula work across Asia-Pacific systems and supplies design implications districts can borrow.
papers.title: A meta-review of literature on educational approaches for teaching AI at the K-12 levels in the Asia-Pacific region
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence (Elsevier)
papers.finding: Meta-review of 14 Asia-Pacific K-12 AI curriculum studies (2018-2021). AI curricula built AI knowledge, skills, attitudes, and interest. Interviews were the most common method. Theories used include holistic models, TPACK, and self-determination theory. Gives implications for standards, curriculum, formal and informal learning, teacher PD, and learning progressions.

papers.why: Gives the secondary half of the AI literacy progression: project based, artifact producing, with a junior to senior split.
papers.title: Artificial intelligence (AI) literacy education in secondary schools: a review
papers.venue: Interactive Learning Environments (Taylor and Francis)
papers.finding: Thematic review of 50 secondary school AI education studies (2016 to 2022). Collaborative project based learning with artifact creation is the most common pedagogy; tools span hardware, software, intelligent agents, and unplugged activities; junior students experience AI and basics, seniors go technical; assessments use knowledge tests, questionnaires, and qualitative artifacts; outcomes measured across affective, behavioral, cognitive, and ethical dimensions.

papers.why: Background.
papers.title: Generative AI-enhanced learning experiences for computational thinking: A systematic scoping review and design guidelines
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Scoping review and design guidelines for GenAI in computational thinking learning.

papers.why: Adds attitudes and self-efficacy to the AI literacy appendix.
papers.title: Artificial intelligence literacy at school: A systematic review with a focus on psychological foundations
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Systematic review of 58 studies defining school AI literacy for teachers, students, and staff; dimensions include cognitive, emotional, and psychological aspects, not only knowledge.

papers.why: Knowledge gaps persist into college.
papers.title: What undergraduate students need to know and actually know about generative AI
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: What undergraduates need to know vs actually know about GenAI.

papers.why: Another framework option for the appendix.
papers.title: Unleashing human potential: An artificial intelligence competency framework for K–12 education
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Scoping review of 54 K-12 AI competency frameworks: foundational knowledge, practical and cognitive skills, ethical awareness; proposes Understanding, Using, Unleashing framework emphasizing human values.

papers.why: Equity-focused framework option.
papers.title: The Scaffolded AI literacy (SAIL) framework: Results of a Delphi study for equitable AI literacy framework design in education
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Delphi study producing the Scaffolded AI Literacy (SAIL) framework for equitable AI literacy design.

papers.why: Youth advisory boards improve AI curricula; integrated science ML units can reduce gaps.
papers.title: Design of a science integrated secondary school AI literacy curriculum: A youth & AI expert guided design-based research approach
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Two-year design-based research on a four-week summer science-integrated machine learning curriculum for high school youth with an alumni and expert advisory board. ML knowledge gains in both cohorts; larger in cohort 2. Female and non-White students tended to gain more than White male peers.

papers.why: Regular classroom teachers can teach AI literacy effectively.
papers.title: An Effectiveness Study of Teacher-Led AI Literacy Curriculum in K-12 Classrooms
papers.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
papers.finding: Teacher-led AI literacy curriculum, 89 middle schoolers vs 69 comparison: deeper AI concept understanding and more positive attitudes toward AI careers.

papers.why: Assessment gap in AI literacy.
papers.title: AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review
papers.venue: International Journal of STEM Education
papers.finding: Review of 179 K-12 AI literacy documents: few assessed whether students learned; calls for a competency framework co-designed with teachers.

papers.why: Ethics and careers fit middle school AI lessons.
papers.title: Integrating Ethics and Career Futures with Technical Learning to Promote AI Literacy for Middle School Students: An Exploratory Study
papers.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
papers.finding: DAILy workshop: middle schoolers learned supervised learning and logic systems, identified and mitigated bias, and connected AI to careers.

papers.why: Design principles for middle school AI units.
papers.title: AI + Ethics Curricula for Middle School Youth: Lessons Learned from Three Project-Based Curricula
papers.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
papers.finding: Three MIT middle school AI + ethics curricula taught by trained in-service teachers using active learning, embedded ethics, and low barriers.

papers.why: Robots are mostly studied with young children in short trials.
papers.title: Artificial intelligence-based robots in education: A systematic review of selected SSCI publications
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Review of SSCI studies on AI robots in education: most target learners under 13, run under 4 weeks, in language and science.

papers.why: Links AI literacy to language arts, so primary schools can teach AI without a separate course.
papers.title: Using digital story writing as a pedagogy to develop AI literacy among primary students
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.caveat: No control group; interviews with 16 top students only.
papers.finding: 82 Hong Kong upper primary students did a three-month digital story writing program about AI. Stories showed understanding of AI concepts (supervised learning, neural networks) and reached the use-and-apply level; students proposed real-life AI solutions.

papers.why: Upper elementary students arrive thinking AI is a thinking person. Lessons should start by demystifying: show the data behind a familiar tool.
papers.title: Finnish 5th and 6th grade students' pre-instructional conceptions of artificial intelligence (AI) and their implications for AI literacy education
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Survey of 195 Finnish grade 5-6 students before instruction. Conceptions of AI were varied and often uninformed; almost no student mentioned data. Many described AI as human-like with human thinking, echoing media portrayals. Authors flag family income and parent education as likely drivers of unequal AI knowledge.

papers.why: Relevant to staff and parent AI literacy.
papers.title: Artificial intelligence literacy in higher and adult education: A scoping literature review
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Scoping review of AI literacy in higher and adult education.

papers.why: Supports team-based AI lessons and local adaptation.
papers.title: The role of learners’ competencies in artificial intelligence education
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Study of Nigerian K-12 learners' competencies for AI education; all hypotheses supported. Teamwork and human-tool collaboration were important for AI literacy; curricula should reflect local context rather than import Western or Eastern designs.

papers.why: Evidence that middle schoolers can handle generative AI and deepfake literacy, which the book needs for its media literacy ideas.
papers.title: Children as creators, thinkers and citizens in an AI-driven future
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 2
papers.finding: 38 middle school students learned generative modeling, how deepfakes are made, cues to spot them, and how misinformation spreads. Students could explain deepfakes and misinformation and formed policy opinions, so these are appropriate goals for this age.

papers.why: Early AI courses should lead with interest and relevance; a gender gap appears already in primary grades.
papers.title: Modeling the structural relationship among primary students' motivation to learn artificial intelligence
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 2
papers.finding: Survey of 420 primary students in Beijing AI curriculum pilot schools. Intrinsic motivation had the strongest influence on career motivation; attention, relevance, and confidence also mattered. Boys scored higher than girls on motivational factors.

papers.why: Concrete elementary unit where students train an image classifier and use it in play.
papers.title: Behavioral-pattern exploration and development of an instructional tool for young children to learn AI
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 2
papers.caveat: Small sample, behavioral sequence analysis only.
papers.finding: 9-week elementary course: 5 weeks individual work in MIT App Inventor with a personal image classifier, 4 weeks pairs building a robot car and playing a computational thinking board game. Testing-and-executing behavior mattered most in cooperative work.

papers.why: Gives the book a simple four-part AI literacy scaffold that fits grade bands and complements Long and Magerko's 17 competencies.
papers.title: Conceptualizing AI literacy: An exploratory review
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 2
papers.caveat: Small evidence base, mostly exploratory; pre-generative AI.
papers.finding: Review of 30 studies proposes four aspects of AI literacy mapped to Bloom's levels: know and understand, use and apply, evaluate and create, and ethics. Most studies targeted primary (14) and secondary (14) students; only 2 targeted teachers. Most were qualitative, exploratory conference papers. Kindergarten assessment used short picture-based multiple-choice items.

papers.why: Shows a short course can build conceptual AI literacy without a technical background; model for staff PD length.
papers.title: Evaluation of an artificial intelligence literacy course for university students with diverse study backgrounds
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 2
papers.finding: 7-hour AI literacy course for 120 university students from many majors; significant gains in AI concept understanding and empowerment for both genders.

papers.why: Gives the book a plain, citable definition of AI literacy and a competency checklist usable from PreK to 12 without requiring coding. Supports narrower, more supervised use for young children.
papers.title: What is AI Literacy? Competencies and Design Considerations
papers.venue: CHI 2020 (ACM)
papers.caveat: 2020, before generative AI chatbots in schools. Scoping review, not empirical testing; competencies are proposals, not validated outcomes.
papers.finding: Defines AI literacy as competencies to critically evaluate AI, communicate and collaborate with it, and use it as a tool. Scoping review of 150 documents yields 17 competencies in five themes (What is AI, What can AI do, How does AI work, How should AI be used, How do people perceive AI) and 15 design considerations. Coding is not a prerequisite; digital literacy is. Children under about 8 overestimate agent intelligence and trust agents as friendly; children first personify agents then learn they are programmable.

papers.why: Teachers new to AI need multiple PD formats and school-level support, not a single workshop. Supports a repeatable district curriculum cycle.
papers.title: Sustainable Curriculum Planning for Artificial Intelligence Education: A Self-Determination Theory Perspective
papers.venue: Sustainability (MDPI)
papers.caveat: Case study in one system, qualitative, no student outcome data; curriculum effectiveness not evaluated.
papers.finding: Interviews with 24 Hong Kong teachers (12 with AI teaching experience, 12 without). Good AI curriculum design combines four approaches (content, product, process, praxis) with teachers as orchestrators. Teachers need autonomy, competence, and relatedness (self-determination theory) to sustain it. Proposes a curriculum development cycle for teachers and curriculum officers.

children.name: Lab Report Feedback Before Grading
children.blurb: Lab report feedback before grading means students get automated feedback on a draft lab report tied to the lab rubric, then revise before the teacher grades the final version.

children.name: Designing Experiments and Using Simulations
children.blurb: This idea uses a school configured AI tool as a coach for three science tasks: helping students design fair experiments, guiding them through simulations of things that would be dangerous, expensive or impossible in a real lab, and generating short misconception probes so teachers can see what students actually believe before a lesson.

children.name: Safety, Reading, and Preparation
children.blurb: This idea is that AI can save teachers time in science, STEM, and computer science by drafting safety materials, leveling reading, and helping with diagrams, but it must never be trusted blindly.

children.name: Local Data Projects
children.blurb: Local data projects have students collect their own observations outdoors, such as plants, animals, weather, or water quality, then use AI to help identify species and organize the data.

children.name: Coding Help That Teaches
children.blurb: Coding help that teaches means an AI tool should explain an error message and ask the student what they think is wrong, rather than supplying corrected code.

children.name: Robotics and Engineering Design
children.blurb: Robotics and engineering design give students real problems where a robot fails to turn or a bridge collapses, and they must work out why.

children.name: Building a Model to Learn How AI Works
children.blurb: Building a model is a way for students to learn how AI works by training a simple tool and testing it on new examples.

children.name: Tracing the Data Behind a Tool
children.blurb: Tracing the data behind a tool means asking students to find out where an AI tool's data came from and to think about what that origin means.

children.name: Ethics and Bias Audit Projects
children.blurb: Ethics and bias audit projects have older students test real AI tools with carefully chosen inputs to see whether different groups are treated differently, then write up findings and propose fixes.

children.name: Science for Every Student
children.blurb: Science for Every Student means using AI to adapt the same science investigation so students with different reading levels, languages, and needs can all take part.

children.name: Planning Labs and Units
children.blurb: Planning labs and units is the practice of using an AI tool to draft candidate labs and unit outlines, then having the teacher check, correct and finish them.

children.name: When Students May Use AI in Science
children.blurb: This idea is that science and computer science teachers need task-specific rules for when students may use AI, just as math teachers do.

children.name: Science Fairs, Careers, and the Lab Behind the Scenes
children.blurb: This idea is that AI can coach students through science fair work and career exploration while teachers use it for lab logistics, but it must not take over the student's project or results.

sections.body: Science, STEM, and computer science are the parts of school where students can learn how AI actually works by building it, testing it, and finding its flaws. In ordinary science and computing work, the book describes AI as a coach that gives feedback on lab reports, helps design experiments, guides students through code errors, and supports science fair projects. It also describes teaching about AI itself, through building simple models, tracing the data behind tools, and auditing tools for bias. The book notes that many students, like the Finnish fifth and sixth graders surveyed before instruction, picture AI as a human-like mind and almost never mention data, even though AI is a pattern finder trained on large amounts of data. Both uses of AI in these subjects share one principle, that the student keeps their hands on the real work.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The book finds that AI as a coach can support lab reports, experiment design, code debugging, and science fair work, and that teaching students about AI through hands-on model building, data tracing, and bias audits is where deeper understanding grows. It reports that AI curricula in the Asia-Pacific region built knowledge, skills, attitudes, and interest, that secondary AI education often uses collaborative project based learning with artifact creation, and that teacher-led AI literacy lessons improved middle school students' understanding and attitudes toward AI careers. What does not work is the coding shortcut, where an AI assistant writes working code on request, assignments look better, and nobody checks whether students can write or debug code on their own, so grades rise while skills stay thin. The book also warns that a list of AI tools in use is not the same as AI literacy, and that none of the science ideas yet has strong evidence. The rule it holds to is that AI should coach the student while the student keeps their hands on the real work, with tools checked so they do not give full solutions and with before and after checks to build local evidence.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: For everyday science teaching, a teacher would go to Lab Report Feedback Before Grading, Designing Experiments and Using Simulations, and Safety, Reading, and Preparation to see how AI can coach without taking over the work. For computing and engineering, Coding Help That Teaches, Robotics and Engineering Design, and Local Data Projects keep students building, testing, and working with real data. To teach about AI itself, Building a Model to Learn How AI Works, Tracing the Data Behind a Tool, and Ethics and Bias Audit Projects move from making a simple model to following the data and checking for bias. A leader or team would use Planning Labs and Units, When Students May Use AI in Science, and Science for Every Student to connect classroom choices to planning, to when students may use AI, and to science for every student. A parent curious about where the work can lead would go to Science Fairs, Careers, and the Lab Behind the Scenes for the chapter's look at science fairs, careers, and the lab behind the scenes.
